introduction-the-bill-shock-reality.core: Cloud bills grow from many small decisions: forgotten resources, oversized instances, data transfer, NAT gateways and log ingestion. Cost management needs visibility (who spends what), accountability (tags and owners), commitments for steady usage and continuous optimisation.

first_principles.problem: The monthly bill jumps 40% and nobody can say why.
truths: Steady usage can be bought cheaper.

analogy.title: An itemised phone bill shared by a family
analogy.story: Without names on each line, nobody changes their behaviour.
analogy.breaks: Phone bills are monthly; cloud costs can spike in hours, so alerts must be fast.

example.title: Investigating a jump
flow: Cost Explorer by service: NAT gateway +$12k
Flow logs: S3 traffic via NAT

check.q: What tool detects unusual spend automatically?

cost-explorer-vs-cost-usage-report-cur.core: Cost Explorer is the interactive UI for trends, filtering, forecasts and rightsizing recommendations at daily or monthly granularity. The Cost and Usage Report (CUR 2.0 via Data Exports) is the most detailed dataset (hourly, per resource, with tags and pricing details) delivered to S3 for Athena, QuickSight or FinOps tools.

first_principles.problem: Finance needs per-team, per-resource hourly cost, which Cost Explorer can't export at that detail.
derivation: Use **Cost Explorer** for exploration and forecasts.

analogy.title: A bank's monthly summary versus the full transaction export
analogy.story: The summary shows trends; the export lets you analyse every transaction.
analogy.breaks: Bank exports are small; CUR can be billions of rows for large orgs.

code.text:
SELECT resource_tags['user_team'] AS team, product_servicecode, sum(line_item_unblended_cost) AS cost
FROM cur
WHERE billing_period = '2026-09'
GROUP BY 1, 2 ORDER BY cost DESC;

check.q: What's the most granular AWS cost dataset?
check.a: The Cost and Usage Report (CUR), with hourly, resource-level line items.

savings-plans-vs-reserved-instances-ris.core: Commitments trade flexibility for discounts (up to ~72%) on 1- or 3-year terms. Compute Savings Plans apply to any EC2 family/region, Fargate and Lambda; EC2 Instance Savings Plans give deeper discounts for one family in one region. Reserved Instances still cover RDS, ElastiCache, OpenSearch and Redshift. Commit to your steady baseline, not your peak.

first_principles.problem: A team buys 3-year RIs for instance types it migrates away from six months later.
derivation: **Ladder** purchases over time; monitor **utilisation and coverage**.

analogy.title: A gym annual membership versus pay-per-visit
analogy.story: Cheaper if you go regularly; wasted if you stop going.
analogy.breaks: Gym memberships can't be resold; some RIs can be sold on the RI marketplace.

example.title: Sizing a Savings Plan
flow: Hourly compute spend: min $40, avg $70, peak $150

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: ~30% saving on baseline with no waste.

check.q: Which commitment covers Lambda and Fargate?

tagging-policies-showback-vs-chargeback.core: Tags (team, env, cost-centre, service) let you attribute cost. Enforce them with tag policies, SCPs and IaC defaults, and activate them as cost allocation tags. Showback reports each team's spend for awareness; chargeback actually bills it to their budget, creating stronger incentives.

first_principles.problem: 40% of spend is untagged, so no team owns it.
truths: Tags must be applied at creation.
Some costs are shared and must be split.
derivation: Use **accounts per team** as the strongest boundary.
Allocate **shared costs** by rule; start with **showback**, move to **chargeback**.

analogy.title: Splitting a restaurant bill
analogy.story: Itemised orders make each person's share clear; shared starters are split by agreement.
analogy.breaks: Diners see the menu prices; teams often don't see cost until reports exist.

check.q: What's the difference between showback and chargeback?
check.a: Showback reports costs to teams for awareness; chargeback bills those costs to their budgets.
